strengths: The work is best assessed primarily as an Applied/Systems contribution with a substantial Datasets/Benchmarks component. Under that framing, unifying nine motion synthesis and comprehension tasks in one autoregressive framework is ambitious and potentially useful; the breadth of integration matters more than introducing an entirely new generative paradigm.

MotionHub consolidates single-person, interaction, dance, and speech-motion data into a common SMPL-H representation. Its reported scale—over 131k single-person motions, 21k two-person motions, and 70 hours of paired audio—could provide valuable infrastructure for multimodal motion research.

The HoMi tokenizer is motivated by the practical cost of residual quantization. On MotionHub, its single 2,048-entry codebook attains reconstruction errors comparable to a six-codebook RVQ and substantially improves over the tested single-codebook alternatives (Table 5).

The component ablation supports both the separate hand/body encoders and frequency-aware gating: removing either worsens reconstruction, while removing both causes a substantial degradation (Table 9). The supplementary experiments also examine motion representation and codebook size.

Several results are promising: MotionLLaMA improves most single-person motion-to-text metrics, substantially improves interaction motion-to-text retrieval, has the strongest interaction text-to-motion retrieval/alignment, and performs well on motion in-betweening and dance-to-music beat metrics.
The paper is generally well organized, provides task-specific evaluation protocols, and includes both quantitative and qualitative results across an unusually broad set of modalities.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim—that one unified model effectively handles all tasks—is not adequately isolated. There is no reported comparison between the unified and stated task-expert variants, no single-task-versus-multitask ablation, and no analysis of negative transfer. It is also unclear which variant produced each table. Consequently, the experiments demonstrate task coverage more clearly than the benefit of unification.

The evaluation protocol for the newly assembled MotionHub benchmark is underspecified. The paper does not clearly define train/validation/test splits, explain whether source-dataset identities or subjects are separated across splits, or rule out overlap among datasets aggregated through MotionX and the other listed sources. Because evaluation encoders are also trained on MotionHub, precise separation and leakage controls are essential.

Several headline claims overstate the tables. On single-person text-to-motion, MotionLLaMA trails multiple methods in R-precision, FID, and multimodal distance (Table 3). On interaction text-to-motion it improves alignment but has markedly worse FID than InterGen. Its AIST++ music-to-dance FID is 58.56 versus 24.34 for M3GPT, and its speech-to-gesture FGD is worse than MCM and DiffStyleGesture (Tables 6 and 8). Thus, “state-of-the-art across an extensive range” is not supported.

The dance-to-music evaluation measures only beat coverage and alignment, despite claiming generation of background music. These metrics do not establish audio quality, musical coherence, or semantic appropriateness and may reward excessive beat production; the perfect 100% coverage especially warrants qualitative or human evaluation.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript omits the exact LLaMA-3.2 model size, batch sizes, sequence lengths and truncation policy, task-sampling ratios, optimizer details beyond learning rate, hardware/compute, dataset splits, evaluation sample counts for most tasks, and a sufficiently precise specification of the tokenizer architecture and losses. Reporting “500 epochs across all tasks” is not enough to reconstruct training.

The empirical results lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is important where claimed gains are small, such as the tokenizer’s advantage over RVQ, and where generative sampling can produce substantial variance.

MotionHub is principally an aggregation and reannotation of existing datasets, but licensing compatibility, redistribution rights, annotation protocol and quality control, annotator statistics, and the effects of GPT-4o recaptioning are not documented adequately. Reported dataset totals are also inconsistent between the main-text contribution statement and Table 10.

The qualitative evidence consists largely of sparse pose snapshots, which cannot substantiate temporal smoothness, audio synchronization, hand fidelity, or generated music quality. No user study is provided. The paper also lacks a meaningful discussion of limitations, demographic bias, consent/privacy, and misuse risks associated with human-motion and speech data.

strengths: The unified scope is ambitious and potentially useful: one autoregressive framework covers nine synthesis and comprehension tasks involving text, motion, speech, music, and two-person interaction.

The HoMi tokenizer has a sensible motivation. Separating body and hand encoders while retaining one codebook could simplify generation, and its reconstruction accuracy is broadly comparable to the six-codebook RVQ baseline.

MotionHub consolidates numerous public motion datasets into a common SMPL-H representation and adds filtering, normalization, and captions. If released with complete documentation, this could be a useful community resource.
The paper reports results across an unusually broad collection of tasks and includes comparisons for both single-person and interactive motion.
weaknesses: The central evidence does not establish that the proposed ingredients cause the reported multitask performance. Ablations only measure tokenizer reconstruction; there are no downstream ablations for HoMi versus standard VQ/RVQ, frequency gating, separate encoders, unconditional pretraining, multitask training, LLM scale, or the unified versus expert models.

The evaluation protocol is materially ambiguous. The paper says that both expert models and one unified model were trained, but never identifies which model produced each table. Train/validation/test splits for the aggregated datasets are also not specified, making leakage difficult to exclude when evaluation is performed on MotionHub components such as AIST++, FineDance, and BEAT2.

Comparisons are not consistently convincing or demonstrably fair. Some baselines are reimplemented on MotionHub, while other numbers appear to come from dataset-specific prior work; implementation details, model capacities, and tuning budgets are not reported. Newly trained TMR and gesture feature extractors are used for evaluation without validation against standard evaluators or evidence that they do not favor the proposed system.

Several claims overstate the tables. MotionLLaMA is not best on single-person text-to-motion and has substantially worse AIST++ music-to-dance FID than several baselines. On interaction text-to-motion it improves alignment but has worse FID than both reported alternatives. The tokenizer only narrowly matches RVQ overall and is worse on several normalized and hand-reconstruction measures, rather than clearly surpassing it.

The dance-to-music result is especially under-supported. Beat-only metrics can be maximized by trivial or poor-quality rhythmic audio, yet no audio fidelity, musicality, semantic relevance, human evaluation, or qualitative audio analysis is provided. A perfect 100.0 beat-coverage score therefore does not substantiate the claimed quality of generated background music.

MotionHub is insufficiently documented for a dataset contribution. There is no precise split policy, deduplication analysis, annotation protocol, annotator information, quality-control statistics, licensing discussion, or release URL. ChatGPT-generated captions are used without prompts or validation. Dataset counts are also inconsistent: the abstract reports 131,515 single-person motions and 21,021 dual-person motions, whereas Table 10 reports 131,512 motions overall and its listed dual-person subsets sum to 19,267.

Reproducibility is poor despite the claim that code and data are publicly available: the manuscript contains a blank source-code footnote. It omits the exact LLaMA-3.2 model size, optimizer and schedule, batch size, sequence construction and truncation, sampling counts, compute requirements, tokenizer losses, detailed FFT/gating equations, and preprocessing specifics. The statement that all tasks were trained for 500 epochs is too ambiguous to reconstruct the training budget.

Results lack repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, and human perceptual studies. The few static qualitative examples cannot demonstrate temporal realism, hand quality, interaction plausibility, or audio-motion synchronization.

The work is largely an integration of LLaMA, LoRA, WavTokenizer, VQ-VAE, and aggregated existing datasets. Integration at this breadth can be valuable, but the limited methodological specification and missing causal ablations leave the technical originality and significance uncertain.

Presentation quality is below publication standard, with grammatical errors, malformed or inconsistent terminology, incomplete citations/links, and contradictions between dataset statistics and claims. Limitations, bias, consent/licensing, and misuse risks for synthesized human motion and speech-conditioned avatars are not discussed. Overall, the breadth and resource potential provide merit, but the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility concerns favor rejection.

strengths: The paper makes a substantial systems contribution by unifying nine motion synthesis and comprehension tasks—including single-person, two-person, full-body, hand, text, speech, and music settings—within one autoregressive framework. Because no contribution type is declared, Algorithms/General is the default, but the work is more appropriately viewed primarily as Applied/Systems with a significant Datasets/Benchmarks component; under that framing, its breadth and integration are meaningful contributions even though the individual algorithmic ingredients are relatively incremental.

MotionHub is a valuable resource: it consolidates and standardizes diverse public datasets and provides 131k-plus single-person motions, approximately 21k two-person motions, extensive captions, and 70.10 hours of paired audio. Its inclusion of full-body and interaction data addresses limitations of motion-language datasets centered on single-person body motion.

The HoMi tokenizer is practically attractive. It obtains reconstruction accuracy comparable to a six-codebook RVQ while using one codebook, and it improves substantially over the reported single-codebook alternatives. The component ablation, codebook-size study, utilization analysis, and comparison of motion representations provide useful supporting evidence.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. MotionLLaMA is particularly strong on motion-to-text and interaction motion-to-text, motion completion/in-betweening, dance-to-music beat metrics, and semantic alignment for two-person text-to-motion. The paper also reports less favorable outcomes rather than restricting evaluation to tasks on which it dominates.

The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly motivates the framework. The appendix adds dataset construction details, metric definitions, representation studies, and qualitative sequences. The stated release of code, visualizations, and MotionHub would make the contribution useful to the community.
weaknesses: The central unified-model claim is not isolated convincingly. The paper says that both task-paired expert models and a model jointly trained on all tasks were produced, but the tables do not clearly identify which model generated each result. There is no expert-versus-unified comparison, analysis of cross-task transfer or interference, or single-task baseline under matched capacity. This ambiguity should be resolved because breadth is the paper's main scientific claim.

Evaluation is largely conducted on the newly assembled MotionHub benchmark using evaluation encoders also trained on MotionHub. The manuscript does not specify dataset splits, subject separation, overlap or duplicate handling among source datasets, or whether evaluation encoders are trained strictly without test data. Since MotionX contains multiple constituent datasets while several datasets are also separately incorporated, explicit leakage and overlap safeguards are important. Baselines are described as replicated, but their common training protocol and tuning budget are not sufficiently documented.

Some headline SOTA claims are broader than the tables support. For two-person text-to-motion, MotionLLaMA has the best retrieval/alignment measures but substantially worse FID than InterGen (0.1133 versus 0.0537). On AIST++ music-to-dance, its FID is 58.56 compared with 24.34 for M3GPT, although alignment and diversity are strong. Speech-to-gesture FGD and diversity are also not competitive with the best baselines. These results still support a versatile system, but the claims should distinguish semantic alignment, fidelity, and diversity more carefully.

The ablations establish improved tokenizer reconstruction but do not show that separate hand/body encoding, frequency-aware gating, a single codebook, or the chosen LLM materially improve downstream generation and comprehension. A matched downstream comparison against vanilla VQ, RVQ plus a suitable generative head, removal of unconditional pretraining, and different LLM scales would make the algorithmic case substantially stronger.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the claimed release. The exact LLaMA-3.2 size, optimizer, batch size, sequence/window lengths, task-sampling ratios, training hardware and duration, number of samples used for each metric, random seeds, and variability are absent. The statement that both stages run for 500 epochs is insufficient for reproducing a heterogeneous multitask training schedule.

MotionHub's curation needs stronger documentation: source licenses and redistribution constraints, annotator protocol and quality agreement, validation of GPT-4o recaptions, and per-source train/test statistics are missing. The main text and appendix also give slightly inconsistent aggregate counts. There is no meaningful discussion of dataset bias, privacy or consent inherited from source motion/audio data, or potential misuse of generated human motion. These issues do not negate the contribution, but they limit confidence in the dataset's benchmark readiness.
